https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-01/g.text: Explore the ABC analysis Global politics is being driven in disturbing directions by more than just strongmen L By Laura Tingle Topic: World Politics Posted Sat 1 Aug 2026 at 5:00am Sat 1 Aug 2026 at 5:00am Sat 1 Aug 2026 at 5:00am Donald Trump's rambling pronouncements barely rate any immediate quiver in world markets, let alone diplomatic circles. ( AP Photo: Julia Demaree Nikhinson ) abc.net.au/news/global-politics-driven-strongmen-disturbing-directions/106982606 Link copied Share Share article For much of the past decade, a lot of what has unfolded in the world has been seen through the idea of the rise of strongmen in global politics. Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin have headed the list, along with Recep Tayyip Erdoğan in Türkiye. And that's not to mention the ones who have come and gone in the meantime: Hungary's Viktor Orbán, Jair Bolsonaro in Brazil, Rodrigo Duterte in the Philippines. But so much has been transformed in the past year. In the United States and Russia, two of the strongmen may still hold unprecedented power within their countries, and seek to exert on the rest of the world, but they do so with rapidly diminishing credibility and effectiveness. Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin have headed the list of strongmen in global politics, along with Xi Jinping. ( Reuters: Kevin Lamarque/File Photo ) Trump's rambling pronouncements — someone described them this week as "fantasy announcements" — barely rate any immediate quiver in world markets, let alone diplomatic circles. For example, there was cautious early reporting in international media on Friday morning, Australian time, of his announcement on social media of a "HISTORIC agreement for the COMPLETE DISARMAMENT of Hamas and all other armed groups in Gaza". As is so often the case these days, everyone immediately wanted to know if anybody else had actually agreed to this agreement. As The New York Times reported: "There was no immediate comment from Hamas or Israel, and it was not clear whether either had signed off on the plan after years of war and a fragile ceasefire." A new conflation of important factors It's not just that some of the strongmen don't seem so strong anymore, that they often just seem to be lashing out reasonably ineffectively, or even that the "Great Powers" don't seem to be running things. It's that there is a new conflation of factors proving to be just as important, if not more so, in driving world events in increasingly disturbing directions. These include the dividend of years of greater powers' efforts at destabilising other states; the rise of states that have never quite got to be stable in the first place; and of the role of non-state actors. More recently there has been the rapidly and relentlessly expanding story of how technological change in warfare — and rapidly diminishing stockpiles of defensive weapons — are transforming geopolitical power. Will Hamas disarm? Experts say 'it's difficult to believe' Middle East analysts are sceptical Hamas will willingly lay down its weapons and that Israel will totally withdraw from Gaza. Just in this week alone, we have seen the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine spread inexorably: conspicuously dragging in Saudi Arabia as well as conflicts in Iraq, Syria and Yemen continuing to escalate. But Egypt has now also found itself under attack. Also, Ukraine directly attacked an Iranian vessel in the Caspian Sea, a move which linked the Iranian and Ukrainian conflicts. It also reflected Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's apparent attempts to highlight Russian support for Iran to the US president days before he went to see Trump in Washington. Then there are reports — denied by the Chinese — of a major deal to deliver Chinese arms to Iran. In Europe, NATO jets scrambled this week as a Russian missile entered Polish airspace and crashed. Ukraine has expressed alarm that North Korea is about to send another 30,000 troops to Russia to support its campaign. Yet even with all this, the impacts of the major conflicts of the time don't just involve crossfire and manpower. Trump scuttles nuclear power deal with Saudi Arabia Russia, one of the world's largest resource economies, is now importing oil from India because of the damage Ukraine has inflicted on its energy infrastructure. The European Union is struggling with a dilemma about placing sanctions on an aluminium smelter in Ireland owned by Russian interests because European nations also need the aluminium. There are reports that Ukraine has been buying Chinese drone components from an EU defence loan. The chaos that Trump's increasingly erratic interventions create was highlighted this week by the announcement of a nuclear power deal with Saudi Arabia — a 30-year legal framework that would let US companies build nuclear infrastructure and export civilian nuclear technology to Saudi Arabia while blocking foreign competitors such as China and Russia. Saudi Arabia must recognise Israel for nuclear deal, says Trump A newly brokered nuclear energy deal between the US and Saudia Arabia has drawn criticism from Israeli officials who say it tempts a nuclear arms race in the Middle East. Critics pointed out some of the alarming shortcomings of the deal. It would allow Saudi Arabia to develop a full-blown civilian nuclear industry (OK so far) but without international safeguards. Unlike stricter historical precedents like the US deal with the United Arab Emirates, reports indicate this agreement may permit Saudi enrichment on its own soil over time. As former director-general of the Australian Safeguards and Non-Proliferation Office John Carlson wrote this week: "This deal compromises both the non-proliferation standards that up to now have been applied by the United States, and the contemporary standard for International Atomic Energy Agency safeguards applied under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT)." And, just saying, it would set up exactly the same ecosystem that the US and Israel find so threatening in Iran when it comes to nuclear power, presumably on the presumption that Saudi will always be a friendly state. Just to confuse things further, Trump then effectively scuttled the deal by saying Saudi would have to sign up to being friends with Israel under the Abraham Accords if the deal were to proceed. Which Saudi won't do. In doing so, Trump only highlighted how insane the whole situation in the Middle East really is. The irony of Israel's invasions The Arab world in general is going to remain conflicted about Israel, and possibly only become more so, as Israel escalates its brutality and ambitions in what are still technically Palestinian territories, and against Palestinian people. That is despite the Gulf states' continuing anxiety about Iran. The ambiguity of Trump's meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu this week showed what a mire both countries are now in, partly because of this conflicted, ambivalent position of so many of Israel's neighbours. Israel may have felt briefly that it had emerged as the new hegemon in the region. And it continues to redefine the language of international affairs by describing invasions into other territories — now Lebanon and Syria as well as Gaza and the West Bank — as "buffer zones". Israel supporting nascent governments in the region, rather than destabilising them, at some point must become an issue. ( Reuters: Ronen Zvulun ) There is an irony in this, as analyst Gregory Gause pointed out in the latest issue of Foreign Affairs magazine. "Netanyahu believes that Israel is safer when its neighbours are weak and divided," Gause writes. "But he misses the fact that Israel's peace treaties with Egypt and Jordan, two consolidated states that can control their borders and prevent the rise of violent non-state actors in their territory, have been the enduring pillars of Israel's security for decades. "Rather than embrace the prospect of a cooperative Lebanese government willing to work against Hezbollah, Israel renewed its war in Lebanon in 2026. "In Syria, Israel captured a so-called buffer zone, encouraged Syrian Druze to resist the new government, armed Druze militias, and struck Syrian army positions — including the headquarters of the Ministry of Defence — in the name of protecting the Druze." Supporting nascent governments in the region, rather than destabilising them, at some point must become an issue. "Iran's allies, although weakened, still wield significant influence across the Arab world. In Iraq's elections in November 2025, Shiite parties aligned with Iran and the Iraqi militias it backs performed well," Gause writes. "In February, March, and April of this year, those militias lobbed missiles at US bases in the region. The new Iraqi government under Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, like its predecessors, has filled important positions with many of Iran's local allies." Which brings us to Iran. Loading A more sophisticated assessment of Iran Two major analysts of Iran, Narges Bajoghli and Vali Nasr, both of Johns Hopkins University, have also written in the latest Foreign Affairs , offering a somewhat more sophisticated assessment of the Iranian leadership and its strategy than we get from Trump's expletive-laden assertions of imminent collapse. The new generation of Iranian leadership, the two men say, "has separated revolution from statecraft". "At home and abroad, it neither espouses revolutionary grandiosity nor advocates revolutionary activism." The new leaders, Bajoghli and Nasr write, are "establishment actors: pragmatic, hardened nationalists operating with a clear-eyed assessment of Iran's capabilities and vulnerabilities". "Unlike their predecessors, they can exercise strategic patience and act decisively. They look at Iran's weaknesses frequently and publicly — something the founding generation was too insecure to do honestly — and they treat them as problems to be solved." Trump vows to hit Iran 'hard' in expletive ridden warning In a phone interview with Fox News, the US president reportedly said the US would "beat the f****** s***" out of Iran in response to the surprise strikes. The Islamic Republic had long operated through a chaotic maze of competing power centres, which produced unending internal debate and sclerotic inertia. But they say this chaos has given way "to organisational discipline and resilience" with a structure involving defence, civilian and economic bureaucracies. As a result, Bajoghli and Nasr say, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice-President JD Vance "are wrong" in their fundamental assessment of Iran. "Tehran's defiant approach reflects neither ideological rigidity nor factional infighting," they write. "The country's leaders understand that the United States is seeking to get from talks what it could not achieve in war and that Washington is not interested in a deal but in Iran's surrender." The only problem is "Iranian leaders already claim they have won the war". "This self-confidence — rooted in the belief that the war has empowered Iran rather than weakened it — is informing their international outlook." Abroad, they say this does not mean it will abandon its regional allies, such as Hezbollah, Shiite militias in Iraq and the Houthis in Yemen. "But it will manage them with more strategic discipline and less ideological romanticism." The new Iranian leadership will not sacrifice Iran's interests at the altar of revolutionary solidarity, Bajoghli and Nasr say. "These alliances will be deployed as part of a coherent regional strategy designed to sustain Iran's strategic depth against sustained US and Israeli pressure." The most important message in that assessment, of course, is that Iran actually has a coherent regional strategy. Something that cannot necessarily be said for the great powers who might like to think they can still call the shots. Laura Tingle is the ABC's Global Affairs Editor. https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: ‘Rubio has vowed to dismantle the ICC “brick by brick, if necessary”.’ Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/Reuters View image in fullscreen ‘Rubio has vowed to dismantle the ICC “brick by brick, if necessary”.’ Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/Reuters Opinion International criminal court With ICC sanctions, Trump wants to make the world safe for war criminals Kenneth Roth The US is engaged in a lawless quest to protect American and Israeli officials Fri 21 Aug 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 08.02 EDT Share T he Trump administration has taken another step in its crusade against the international criminal court by imposing sanctions on two more senior ICC officials. The growing number of sanctioned jurists – now 13 – does not change the lawless nature of this quest. Donald Trump and his henchman, Marco Rubio, want to make the world safe for US and Israeli war criminals. No one should let them. The latest victims of Trump’s vendetta are the ICC president – its chief judge, Tomoko Akane of Japan – and Abdoulaye Seye of Senegal, a senior ICC trial lawyer, evidently for his role advancing the prosecution of Israeli officials. Yet the real victims are not these particular individuals, but people worldwide who look to the court as one of the few avenues of recourse against unscrupulous leaders who commit mass atrocities such as fighting wars by targeting civilians. Why does the US want to ‘dismantle’ the international criminal court? | Kenneth Roth Read more We should never let Trump normalize these sanctions. Their main effect is to deprive the target of the ability to use the international financial system – no credit cards, no access to banks, extreme difficulty navigating a modern economy. That is a tool once reserved for corrupt or violent officials who were otherwise beyond the law. Trump is using them to attack the public officials who would bring such heinous individuals to justice. Rubio, the secretary of state, dressed up the sanctions with high-sounding rhetoric about the ICC threatening “ America sovereignty ”. That is true only if Americans (and Israelis) have a sovereign right to commit war crimes wherever they want. Even Rubio cannot get himself to spell out what King Trump’s campaign is really about. Rubio’s main articulated complaint is that the ICC can “investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute officials whose government has not consented to ICC jurisdiction”. That is true, but it is wrong only if one adopts a conveniently (for Washington and the Israeli government) narrow sense of how the court should obtain jurisdiction for a crime. On the one hand, when a country joins the ICC, it accepts the court’s jurisdiction over its citizens. That might be called jurisdiction by virtue of nationality. The US government accepts that route to jurisdiction because it never joined the court. But when a country becomes a court member, it also confers jurisdiction over crimes on its territory, even when committed by a foreigner. That is hardly controversial. A hallmark of sovereignty is the ability to enforce the law on a country’s own territory. Even the Trump administration would not dare object to, say, the British government prosecuting an American for a crime committed in London. But the administration claims it is somehow an outrage if a country confers that same territorial jurisdiction on the ICC for war crimes and similar atrocities committed by foreigners on its territory – a major purpose of the court. The US government objected to such territorial jurisdiction when the court’s treaty was adopted at a major diplomatic conference in Rome in 1998 – and lost overwhelmingly, by a vote of 120 to seven. Since then, even the US government has accepted territorial jurisdiction when convenient. After the ICC used it to prosecute Vladimir Putin (Russia never joined the court) for the kidnapping of children from Ukraine (a member), Joe Biden called the prosecution “ justified ”. The late senator Lindsey Graham, a Republican leader on foreign policy, orchestrated a unanimous Senate resolution in support. Donald Trump and his henchman, Marco Rubio, want to make the world safe for US and Israeli war criminals. No one should let them But for Trump, territorial jurisdiction suddenly became toxic again when it was used to charge Benjamin Netanyahu and the former Israeli defense minister Yoav Gallant with deliberately starving and depriving Palestinian civilians in Gaza. Israel is not a member of the ICC, but Palestine, where the alleged crimes took place, is. Territorial jurisdiction can also be used to charge foreigners from non-member states with aiding and abetting crimes in a state where the ICC has jurisdiction. For example, the court might charge United Arab Emirates officials with aiding and abetting genocide in the Darfur region of Sudan by sending arms and mercenaries to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, Rwandan officials with aiding and abetting war crimes in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo by arming and supporting the M23 rebel group, or US officials (Trump’s real concern) with aiding and abetting Israel’s genocide in Gaza by supplying arms and military aid. Indeed, territorial jurisdiction means that the sanctions themselves could lead to prosecution of Trump and Rubio. Article 70 of the Rome Statute, the ICC’s founding treaty, codifies the crime of obstructing justice when someone retaliates “against an official of the Court on account of duties performed”. That’s exactly what the Trump-Rubio sanctions do. The court would have jurisdiction because the sanctions relate to the prosecution of Israeli officials for crimes committed on Palestinian territory. Rubio has vowed to dismantle the ICC “brick by brick, if necessary”, announcing : “We expect more countries to join our campaign by ending their funding and participation in this politicized and unaccountable court.” Yet that bombast so far has produced few results among the court’s 125 members. Trump says he will dismantle the ICC ‘brick by brick’. It could be his most chilling move of all | Steve Bloomfield Read more Venezuela, which has become a US vassal state since Trump’s seizure of Nicolás Maduro, has announced its withdrawal. So has Chad, which announced its departure after a call from a state department official. But Chadian officials have their own reasons to worry about the court because they allowed their territory to be used by the UAE to arm the RSF in Sudan. (Separately from Trump’s campaign, three military juntas in the Sahel have also announced their exit from the ICC: Niger , Mali and Burkina Faso .) Yet if the response to the Trump administration’s call to leave the court so far has been tepid, the defense of the court by its supposed closest defenders has not exactly been vigorous. The European Union has what is known as a “ blocking statute ”, legislation designed to negate the application of US sanctions in Europe by prohibiting European banks from complying. But while the EU says it “ deeply regrets ” these new sanctions on the ICC, it has not invoked the blocking statute to protect court personnel. One reason appears to be fear among banks, particularly in the Netherlands, of retaliation from Trump. The ICC is located in the Hague, also the Dutch seat of government. In other words, as European officials see it, fighting genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity is important. Trump’s efforts to allow Americans and Israelis to commit these crimes with impunity is disgraceful. But if defending the rule of law might put Dutch banks in Trump’s crosshairs, justice can wait. The EU can do better than that. Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c1mv.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Ayten Bicer and Hayri Bicer's two children are missing By James Gregory Published 31 August 2026 Ayten Bicer felt her 12-year-old daughter slip from her grasp and disappear as the ferry they were travelling on capsized off the coast of northern Cyprus on Sunday, killing eight people. Her daughter Miray and six-year-old son Memhet Asaf are among 20 people still missing after the vessel sunk while en route to Turkey from the coastal town of Kyrenia, in the self-proclaimed Turkish republic on Cyprus. She and her husband Hayri survived, and like many other families are waiting for news of their loved ones back in port as rescuers continue to search. "She was saying, 'Don't let go'. And I didn't let go of my daughter. I swear, I didn't let her go," Bicer told reporters through tears. Bicer said a suitcase fell on top of her, which forced her daughter from her grip. She managed to grab hold of her daughter's foot, but her shoes were coated in engine oil from the overturned vessel and she slipped through her hands. "It was slippery everywhere. It was like oil. She slipped out of my hand," she recalled. The family was returning to Turkey after a holiday on the Mediterranean island. "We couldn't intervene, we lost our children," Hayri Bicer said. "Two of my three children are gone. We left them. We are leaving them on this island as we go." The vessel had been carrying 259 passengers and eight crew members. Nineteen passengers are currently being treated in hospitals in northern Cyprus, local authorities say. The eight crew members, including the ship's captain, and one other man were formally arrested on Monday. They will be detained for three days, while warrants have been issued for several other people. The privately owned ferry left the popular holiday resort of Kyrenia at about 12:30 (09:30 GMT), en route to the town of Tasucu in Turkey. It had been scheduled to travel to Turkey on Saturday but its journey was delayed due to severe storms hitting the island. The seas were still rough on Sunday. Some eyewitness accounts say the double-hulled ferry jolted violently before slamming onto the sea surface, with part of its bow bursting open on impact. Ãnal Ãstel, prime minister of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC), which is only recognised by Turkey, told local media the boat was hit by two waves before it capsized. While the captain of the vessel was trying to recover from the first wave, a second wave hit and it began taking on water, he said. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Survivors continue to wait for news of their missing relatives at the port in Kyrenia The boat has completely sunk and is lying at a depth of 514m (1,686ft), officials say. Debris remains scattered across the water, including a black wheelie suitcase bobbing on the surface and a sheet of steel that appeared to have broken away from the ferry. Authorities are attempting to recover the vessel's black box recorder to establish what happened. A ship will be arriving from Turkey on Tuesday to help with search efforts, TRNC President Tufan Erhurman said. Meanwhile, a three-day period of national mourning began on Monday. The ferry - a high-speed 40m long, 10m wide Filo Jet vessel - sails under the flag of Turkey, according to Marine Traffic. Filo Denizcilik, the company which operates the capsized passenger boat, said it was "deeply saddened by the tragic accident". The TRNC controls the northern third of the island of Cyprus, which has been divided since 1974. https://bnn-news.com/money/stevedoring-c.text: Photo: Ivars Soikāns/LETA Advertisements The Latvian Stevedoring Companies Association (LSA) has sharply criticised the National Alliance’s (NA) proposed ban on the transit of Russian grain, arguing that behind the loud political slogans there are still no calculations demonstrating that such a move would actually weaken Russia rather than Latvia’s economy. A political slogan alone is not enough to justify a decision whose consequences could affect Latvia’s ports, railway sector, businesses and the state budget. The consequences of such a rushed decision could cost Latvia hundreds of millions of euros. International food traders have already signed contracts for cargo transportation through Latvia, meaning that a sudden ban could create risks of legal action and compensation claims. A decline in cargo volumes could also lead to job losses and require additional state funding to maintain the railway network. Ports and railways must continue to be maintained even if cargo volumes decline – the costs do not disappear. As a result, an increasing share of those costs would have to be borne by the remaining cargo flows, making exports more expensive for Latvian producers as well. The United Nations has also repeatedly emphasised the importance of Russian and Ukrainian food exports to global food security, meaning that the consequences of restricting such flows would extend beyond Latvia. Advertisements LSA rejects the National Alliance’s claim that transit cargo leaves insufficient capacity at ports for Latvian grain. According to the Association, capacity for domestic grain is available at all three major ports, with locally produced grain given priority during the harvest season. The Prime Minister has also confirmed that there are no concerns about port capacity. LSA therefore argues that claims suggesting transit cargo is taking space away from Latvian grain are misleading the public. If Latvia unilaterally bans this transit, the cargo will not disappear – it will simply move to other ports and transport corridors. According to LSA, such a decision should be coordinated at least at the Baltic or EU level. A unilateral Latvian ban would not stop Russian exports but would weaken Latvia’s competitive position. Russian grain would continue reaching buyers, while Latvia would lose cargo, jobs and revenue. Therefore, before such a decision is taken, LSA says the National Alliance should answer one simple question: how many millions would this ban actually take away from Russia, and how many hundreds of millions could it cost Latvia? https://www.dw.com/en/oregon-school-shoo.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OLmo The shooting occurred at the Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon Image: Joe Kline/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Police in the northwestern US state of Oregon have identified a teenage gunman who shot dead four people at a school as a former special needs student there, while praising people who stepped in to stop more killings. Three children aged 5, 8 and 11 lost their lives in Thursday's rampage, along with a 25-year-old female teacher, before the shooter was shot dead by a father of two pupils at the school, located in the town of Bend. Another young child and a teacher were also injured in the attack. Who intervened to prevent more deaths in Oregon? A man in a vehicle outside the school who was shot at and missed by the 16-year-old gunman was the first to alert police to the danger. Before they arrived, however, a female teacher tackled the shooter after he had already killed the victims with a pump-action 12-gauge shotgun in the school's special needs classroom. While the two wrestled with each other, a man identified by family as Kaylub Giamanco, a 36-year-old father of two girls at the school, rushed in with his legally held weapon and shot the gunman dead. "He heard shooting and saw a teacher involved in a physical altercation with the suspect ... and fired his weapon, striking the suspect multiple times," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz told reporters. "When someone is willing to risk their own life for others, we recognize that. The teacher who is willing to stand and fight for her children ... incredible. That is true heroism, and we don't see that a lot in society," he said. The shooting has shocked the Bend community Image: ABC affiliate KOHD/Handout/REUTERS Praise from Trump as gun control debate revived Giamanco's mother told the local branch of Fox News that she was "very proud" and that her son was "an absolute hero." US President Donald Trump also hailed Giamanco's actions. "It's a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it," he told reporters. The shooting in Bend has triggered the usual responses from both sides in the everlasting debate about gun control laws in the US. The National Rifle Association (NRA), one of the main and most powerful opponents of tighter laws on the possession of weapons by civilians, hailed the actions of the armed bystander. "Yesterday's terrible act of violence in Oregon serves as another reminder of the importance of a law-abiding armed citizenry," the NRA said in a post on X. Gun control advocates, however, once more condemned the relative ease with which firearms can be procured in the US, which they see as the main factor in the country's high rate of gun-related deaths compared with most other developed countries. "America's gun violence crisis is killing our babies. Enough is enough," gun-control group GIFFORDS said. According to an analysis by the education information portal Education Week, there have been 26 shootings at US schools so far this year that have resulted in injuries or deaths. More than 360 mass shootings have been recorded across the country this year, according to the Gun Violence Archive. It defines mass shootings as incidents in which at least four people are shot, excluding the shooter. Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAP Australia news Mother sought advice from Alan Jones after broadcaster’s alleged indecent assault of her son, court hears Jones, 85, has pleaded not guilty to 21 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching Listen to the podcast Alan Jones on Trial Amanda Meade Media correspondent Thu 22 Oct 2026 23.24 EDT Last modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 02.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The mother of the youngest alleged victim of Alan Jones continued to seek advice from the broadcaster after the teenager was allegedly indecently assaulted at Jones’s Fitzroy Falls farm, a Sydney court has heard. The divorced mother told the Downing Centre court she had developed a pattern of not trusting herself and she continued her correspondence with Jones because: “I knew he knew about everything; he had an opinion about everything. “I was in a web of dependency with Mr Jones,” the witness said on her last day in the witness box on Friday. Alan Jones on trial: Alleged victim’s mother ‘trusted’ Jones | Week 11 - podcast Read more She previously said she corresponded with Jones after he allegedly kissed the 17-year-old and put his tongue inside his mouth out of fear Jones would withdraw his financial support. During cross examination, defence barrister Claire O’Neill suggested the mother continued to correspond with Jones not because she was scared but because she wanted more money out of him. O’Neill asked: “You did not continue to communicate with Mr Jones because you were scared of his influence over your finances, did you?” The witness replied: “I absolutely was.” Her son, complainant A, is one of five men who allege Jones, 85, sexually touched or indecently assaulted them between 2003 and 2020. All five have now completed their evidence. Jones has pleaded not guilty to 21 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Under cross-examination by the defence, the witness agreed she wrote to Jones about her son’s late university application, a superannuation payment, outstanding legal fees and attaining a Sydney Cricket Ground membership for her son. She was shown an email in which she provided Jones with an update on her son’s university application. The defence asked: “You wanted to lay the groundwork for having Mr Jones pay the [legal] bill?” The mother said the suggestion was “absolute rubbish” and she was “proud of him” for finishing year 12 under difficult circumstances and wanted to convey that in the email. She agreed she sent Jones information about the cost of repairs to her Land Rover but denied she was asking him to pay the bill. “You have told lies in this court about why you continued to have contact with Jones?” O’Neill asked. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion The witness replied: “Absolutely disagree, that’s rubbish.” O’Neill: “You were taking advantage of Mr Jones’s generosity for as long as you could?” Witness: “Absolute rubbish.” When she was asked why she shared personal information with Jones about the deterioration of her relationship with her son she became emotional. “My son, who was a child, suffered trauma and didn’t share it with anyone and it had an effect on his relationship with me and a lot of other people.” Asked by prosecutor Georgina Wright what that trauma was, she replied: “I was referring to what happened to him at Fitzroy Falls”.
